## What it is

The ordinary availability bias is about *levels*: you overestimate how common something is because examples come easily to mind. The second-order version is about *relationships*: you assume that a correlation you see among the people around you holds in the population as a whole.

Gelman's example comes from his work on income and voting. Journalists living among affluent, highly educated Democrats in big coastal cities concluded that rich people in general vote Democratic. Nationally, and especially in poorer states, income is strongly associated with voting Republican.

## Why it matters

Your social circle is not a random sample. It is selected on geography, education, occupation and age, and these are exactly the kinds of variables that change how other variables relate. A correlation that is real in your circle can be weaker, absent or reversed elsewhere. Pundits, researchers and policymakers who reason from their own environment end up with confident and wrong models of society.

## How it works

Suppose the slope of $y$ on $x$ varies by context $c$: $\mathrm{E}(y \mid x, c) = \alpha_c + \beta_c x$. Your experience samples one context, so you learn $\beta_{c_\text{you}}$. The population relationship averages over contexts. It also includes the *between*-context relationship, so it can differ from your local slope in size and even in sign. The fix is to sample broadly, or to model the variation in $\beta_c$ explicitly.

## Simulated example

Forty states, each with its own slope of "votes Republican" on income. The slopes are steep in poorer states and nearly flat in richer ones. You live in one state and observe 200 acquaintances. Compare the slope you see with the slope in the whole country.

```{ojs}
import {rng, range, mean, lm, invLogit, fmt} from "../js/stats.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof myState = Inputs.range([1, 40], {value: 38, step: 1, label: "Your state (1 = poorest, 40 = richest)"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 16, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
nation = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  return range(40).flatMap(s => {
    const wealth = (s - 19.5) / 20;                 // -1 .. 1
    const slope = 0.9 - 0.85 * (wealth + 1) / 2;   // steep in poor states, ~flat in rich
    const alpha = -0.4 * wealth;
    return range(400).map(() => {
      const inc = r.normal(wealth, 1);
      return {state: s + 1, inc, vote: r.bernoulli(invLogit(alpha + slope * inc))};
    });
  });
}
mine = nation.filter(d => d.state === myState).slice(0, 200)
fits = ({
  mine: lm(mine.map(d => d.inc), mine.map(d => d.vote)).b,
  nation: lm(nation.map(d => d.inc), nation.map(d => d.vote)).b
})
```

```{ojs}
binned = (data, label) => range(8).map(k => {
  const lo = -3 + k * 0.75, pts = data.filter(d => d.inc >= lo && d.inc < lo + 0.75);
  return {who: label, inc: lo + 0.375, p: pts.length > 5 ? mean(pts.map(d => d.vote)) : NaN};
}).filter(d => Number.isFinite(d.p))
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  height: 300,
  x: {label: "Income (standardized)", grid: true},
  y: {label: "Share voting Republican", domain: [0, 1], grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, range: ["#d6604d", "#2166ac"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line([...binned(mine, "Your acquaintances"), ...binned(nation, "Whole country")], {x: "inc", y: "p", stroke: "who", strokeWidth: 2, marker: "circle"})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<div class="sim-readout">${md`Slope of vote on income among your acquaintances: **${fmt(fits.mine, 3)}**. In the whole country: **${fmt(fits.nation, 3)}**. Move "your state" to the poor end and your personal experience starts to match the country. Move it to the rich end and your experience suggests income barely matters.`}</div>`
```

## Key takeaways

::: takeaways
- Correlations, not just frequencies, are distorted by the non-random sample of people you know.
- Relationships vary by context. Your local slope is one draw from a distribution of slopes.
- Check intuitions about associations against broad, representative data, and model the variation.
:::
